statement: A very large floor is tiled with regular hexagons and equilateral triangles, all with the same side length. Every side of every hexagon is shared with a triangle, and every side of every triangle is shared with a hexagon. Ignoring the edges of the floor, how many triangles are there for each hexagon?

choices.misconception: I saw that two triangles and two hexagons meet at every corner, so I thought there must be equally many of each shape.
I counted the 6 triangles around each hexagon but forgot that each triangle also touches 3 hexagons, so every triangle was counted 3 times.
I counted the 3 hexagons around each triangle and gave that as the number of triangles for each hexagon.
I counted the sides correctly but turned the ratio upside down, giving hexagons for each triangle.

hints: Count the sides where a hexagon meets a triangle.
Overcount, then correct: count the shared sides once from the hexagons and once from the triangles. Both counts describe the same sides, so set them equal.
Each hexagon has 6 shared sides and each triangle has 3, and every shared side belongs to exactly one of each.

solutions.reliable: Every side on the floor is shared by one hexagon and one triangle. Counting these sides from the hexagons gives 6 for each hexagon, and counting them from the triangles gives 3 for each triangle. Both counts describe the same sides, so 6 x (number of hexagons) = 3 x (number of triangles), and there are 2 triangles for each hexagon. The transferable idea: count the same things from two sides and set the counts equal.
solutions.elegant: Count corners instead. Each hexagon has 6 corners and each corner is shared by 2 hexagons, so there are 3 corners for each hexagon. Each triangle has 3 corners, each shared by 2 triangles, so there are 1.5 corners for each triangle. Hence triangles are twice as many as hexagons.

whyOnTest: Tiling questions often hide a double count, and the tempting wrong answers count each shared tile more than once or read the ratio backwards.
